content.text: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves
Introduction

Not all waves are the same. The way particles move relative to the direction of wave travel defines two main types: transverse and longitudinal waves. Understanding this difference is key to explaining why some waves can do things that others cannot.
Key Concepts
Transverse Waves
Transverse waves
have oscillations perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer.

attrs.alt: Transverse wave showing crests and troughs with particle motion perpendicular to wave direction

content.text: Particles move up and down (or side to side)
Wave travels forward
Creates crests (peaks) and troughs
Examples of Transverse Waves
Light and all electromagnetic waves
Water waves (surface waves)
Waves on a string or rope
S-waves (secondary seismic waves)
Stadium "Mexican" waves
Longitudinal Waves
Longitudinal waves
have oscillations parallel to the direction of energy transfer.

attrs.alt: Longitudinal wave showing compressions and rarefactions with particle motion parallel to wave direction

content.text: Particles move back and forth in the same direction as the wave
Creates compressions (particles close together) and rarefactions (particles spread apart)
Examples of Longitudinal Waves
Sound waves
Ultrasound
P-waves (primary seismic waves)
Waves in a slinky spring (pushed along its length)
Pressure waves in fluids
Key Concept:
The key difference between transverse and longitudinal waves is the direction of oscillation relative to the direction of energy transfer. Transverse = perpendicular; longitudinal = parallel.
Comparing Transverse and Longitudinal Waves

rows.label: Oscillation Direction
rows.left: Perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
rows.right: Parallel to the direction of energy transfer

rows.label: Examples

Wavelength in Each Type
In Transverse Waves
Wavelength = distance from crest to crest (or trough to trough)
In Longitudinal Waves
Wavelength = distance from compression to compression (or rarefaction to rarefaction)
Polarisation
What is Polarisation?
Polarisation
restricts the oscillations of a transverse wave to a single plane.
Only transverse waves can be polarised
Longitudinal waves cannot be polarised (oscillations are already in one line)
Unpolarised Light
Normal light oscillates in all planes perpendicular to the direction of travel.

attrs.alt: Diagram showing unpolarised light passing through a polarising filter to become polarised light

content.text: Polarised Light
Polarised light oscillates in only one plane.
Polarising Filters
A polarising filter only allows oscillations in one plane through
Two polarising filters at 90° to each other block all light
Polaroid sunglasses reduce glare by filtering polarised reflected light
Polarisation as Evidence
The fact that light can be polarised proves it is a transverse wave, not longitudinal.
Worked Examples
Example 1:
Classify each wave as transverse or longitudinal: a) A wave on a guitar string b) The sound from a guitar c) Radio waves d) Waves in a slinky pushed and pulled along its length
Solution:

a) Transverse (string moves up/down, wave travels along string) b) Longitudinal (air particles vibrate parallel to sound direction) c) Transverse (all EM waves are transverse) d) Longitudinal (coils move back/forth along the slinky's length)
Example 2:
Two polarising filters are aligned. Describe what happens as one filter is rotated through 90°.
Solution:
At 0°: Maximum light passes through (planes aligned)
As filter rotates: Less light passes through
At 45°: Approximately half the light intensity
At 90°: No light passes through (planes perpendicular)
Exam Tip:

If a question asks you to prove that light is a transverse wave, describe the polarisation experiment: pass light through two polarising filters and rotate one. The light intensity dropping to zero at 90 degrees proves the wave is transverse.
Example 3:
Explain why sound cannot be polarised.
Solution:

Sound is a longitudinal wave. The air particles vibrate back and forth in the same direction as the wave travels. Polarisation involves restricting oscillations to one plane perpendicular to the wave direction, but longitudinal waves don't oscillate perpendicular to their direction of travel—they oscillate parallel to it. Therefore, there's no plane to restrict.
Sound Waves in Detail
How Sound Travels
A vibrating source (e.g., speaker) pushes air particles forward
These particles push on neighbouring particles (compression)
Particles then move back, creating a rarefaction
The pattern of compressions and rarefactions travels through the air
Our eardrums detect these pressure variations
Sound Cannot Travel Through a Vacuum
Sound requires a medium (particles) to travel through. In space, there's no medium, so there's no sound.
Common Mistake:

Students often confuse compressions and rarefactions. A compression is where particles are squashed together (high pressure), like a crowd pushing together. A rarefaction is where particles are spread apart (low pressure), like the crowd stretching out.
Electromagnetic Waves in Detail
Nature of EM Waves
EM waves consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields:
Electric field oscillates in one plane
Magnetic field oscillates perpendicular to the electric field
Both perpendicular to the direction of travel
No medium required
Why EM Waves Travel Through Vacuum
EM waves don't require particles—they are oscillating fields that regenerate each other as they travel.
Real-World Applications
Polaroid Sunglasses
Light reflected from horizontal surfaces (roads, water) is partially polarised horizontally
Polaroid sunglasses have vertical polarising filters
They block horizontally polarised glare
Reduce eye strain and improve visibility
LCD Screens
Use polarised light
Liquid crystals rotate the plane of polarisation
Allows control of which pixels appear bright or dark
Seismic Waves
P-waves (primary):
Longitudinal, travel through solids and liquids, faster
S-waves (secondary):
Transverse, travel through solids only, slower
The absence of S-waves through Earth's core proves it's liquid
3D Cinema
Two images projected with different polarisations
Glasses have different polarising filters for each eye
Each eye sees a different image, creating 3D effect
Common Misconceptions
"All waves are the same type"
— There are two fundamentally different types based on oscillation direction.
"Longitudinal waves have no wavelength"
— They do! Wavelength is compression to compression.
"Water waves are purely transverse"
— Surface water waves are actually a combination; particles move in circular paths.
"Sound can travel through space"
— Sound needs a medium. Space is a vacuum, so sound cannot travel through it.
"Polarisation blocks half the light"
— Unpolarised light passing through a single polariser loses half its intensity. Two aligned polarisers pass the remaining light; two perpendicular polarisers block all light.
Practice Problems
State whether each of the following is transverse or longitudinal: a) Microwaves b) Ultrasound c) Ripples on a pond d) Earthquake P-waves e) Earthquake S-waves
Describe the difference between a compression and a rarefaction in a longitudinal wave.
Describe an experiment you could carry out to show that light is a transverse wave.
Explain why sound cannot travel from the Sun to Earth, but light can.
Explain how polarising sunglasses reduce glare from a wet road.
In a longitudinal wave, particles oscillate between points 2 cm apart and the compressions are 0.5 m apart. State: a) the amplitude b) the wavelength
Explain why the fact that S-waves cannot travel through liquid provides evidence that Earth's outer core is liquid.
Summary
Transverse waves:
Oscillations perpendicular to wave direction (light, water waves)
Longitudinal waves:
Oscillations parallel to wave direction (sound)
Transverse waves have crests and troughs
Longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions
Only transverse waves can be polarised
Sound needs a medium; EM waves don't
Polarisation proves light is transverse
Applications: sunglasses, LCD screens, 3D cinema, seismology

Compression:
region where particles are pushed close together (high pressure).
Rarefaction:
region where particles are spread apart (low pressure). (definition)
Pass light through two polarising filters.
Rotate one filter through 90°. If the light intensity drops to zero at 90°, the light must be transverse, because only transverse waves can be polarised. (experimental design)
Sound is a mechanical wave
that needs a medium (particles) to travel through. Space is a vacuum with no particles, so sound cannot propagate.
Light is an electromagnetic wave
that does not require a medium and can travel through a vacuum. (comparison)
Light reflected from a wet road is partially polarised

in the horizontal plane. Polarising sunglasses have a vertical transmission axis, so they block the horizontally polarised glare while still allowing other light through. (application of polarisation)

Amplitude = 1 cm
— particles oscillate 2 cm total, so maximum displacement from rest = 2/2 = 1 cm (halving) b)
Wavelength = 0.5 m
— distance between successive compressions equals one wavelength (definition)

that would require them to pass through the core. Since S-waves are transverse and cannot travel through liquids (liquids cannot support shear forces), the absence of S-waves through the core proves it is liquid. (reasoning from evidence)
